name: Combat
content:
When combat or some other tense situation arises and it becomes necessary to track the action carefully, special rules apply governing characters' actions.

It is the GM's responsibility to decide when the game should move into and out of combat.

ENTERING COMBAT

To enter combat, follow these steps:

1) GROUP COMBATANTS

Start by dividing all combatants into GROUPS. A group is a unit of allied combatants who act together as combat progresses. Often there will be just two groups: player characters and foes. In more complex situations, the GM may choose to create additional groups: allies, additional foes, non-combatants, or even environmental factors like a collapsing bridge, an erupting volcano, etc.

If players characters are separated by a significant distance or are otherwise divided in a way that would prevent them from coordinating their efforts, the GM should create multiple groups of player characters.

Once combat groups are established, it's time to establish initiative:

2) ROLL INITIATIVE

To determine the INITIATIVE order among the groups, each member of each group rolls one fate die (d12) and adds their WITS score to the result. Add together the highest result and lowest result among the group's members to determine that group’s total initiative result (the middling results, if any, are not used).

If a group only includes a single combatant, its single initiative roll is the total for its group.

Compare all groups' total initiative results to determine the initiative order for the combat. If there is a tie, each tied group rolls a single fate die as a tiebreaker.

Initiative rolls that produce Sol 🌞 or Morte 💀 contribute to BANE/BOON for the Quest, and Morte 💀 triggers a Soft Move from GM, as with skill checks.

Any combatant that rolls Morte 💀 on their initiative roll is caught off guard and may not during the first regular round of combat, nor can they act during the surprise round:

3) SURPRISE ROUND

Before combat begins in earnest, there may be a SURPRISE ROUND.

Any combatant that rolls Sol 🌞 on their initiative roll gets to act during the surprise round. Only the combatant that rolled Sol 🌞 - not their whole group - gets to act in the surprise round. Any number of combatants from any number of groups may act in the surprise round.

In the surprise round, combatants take turns individually rather than in groups. Compare individual initiative rolls to determine the order of turns for the surprise round.

If a group wants to attempt an ambush, each member of the ambushing group rolls Stealth and each member of the target group rolls Awareness. For each group, add together the highest and lowest result among members to get that group's total. If the ambushing group's total is higher, each member of that group automatically gets to act in the surprise round, regardless of their initiative roll for the combat. Otherwise, roll initiative as normal.

ROUNDS OF COMBAT

Combat progresses in ROUNDS. Each round represents 5 seconds of in-game time, and each group gets the initiative once per round.

When a group has the initiative, each member of the group takes a turn - in whatever order they choose among themselves - before moving on to the next group. The order of turns among members of a group may vary from round to round.

TAKING A TURN

Each combatant has the following options available to them on each of their turns:

  • MOVEMENT: You may move a distance up to your Speed. You can break up your movement, moving before, after or in between actions. Any combination is fine as long as your total movement for the turn is no more than your Speed.

  • SPEND ACTIONS: By default, combatants have 1 ½ actions available to them per round. Many abilities cost one action or one half action to activate. There are also some standard combat actions that are always available to all combatants (see Combat Actions below). You may use any combination of actions and/or half actions each turn. For example, a character with 1 ½ actions could activate one ability that costs an action and another ability that costs a half action, or they could active three different abilities that each cost a half action. Various effects may increase or decrease a combatant's available actions.

  • REACTIONS: By default, combatants have 1 reaction available to them per round. Reactions are special abilities that have a specified trigger condition and may be activated at any time during combat (not just on your turn). In addition to any reaction abilities you may have, all combatants may spend a reaction to make an opportunity attack (see Reach & Opportunity Attacks below).

  • FREE ACTIONS: Combatants may take any number of free actions on their turn. Some abilities are free actions, but free actions also encompass such activities as brief communication, gestures, or simple interactions with objects, like opening or closing a door, pulling a lever, picking up or dropping an item, sheathing or pulling out a weapon, etc. The GM decides what can be reasonably accomplished via free actions on a given turn.

By default, you have 1½ actions per round, and one reaction per round. Some abilities may increase or reduce actions or reactions, permanently or temporarily. Some formidable foes may have more than the standard amount of actions or reactions.

COMBAT ACTIONS

In addition to spending actions to activate your character's abilities, the following options are always available to you in combat. Each costs 1 action:

ATTACK - You make a single melee or ranged attack. Describe your attack.

SPRINT - You move up to your Speed. This is in addition to your normal movement for the turn. Describe your sprint.

HELP - You grant a +1d bonus to another creature's next skill check for a specific task this round. The GM determines whether the task is something you can reasonably help with. Describe how you help.

EVADE - Choose one: 1) You avoid opportunity attacks this turn. 2) Until your next turn, your Dexterity checks are favored, and attacks against you from combatants you can see are ill-favored. Either way, describe how you evade.

SKILL CHECKS IN COMBAT

When you attempt to perform an action in combat that is neither an ability nor one of the combat actions above, the GM may call for a skill check to determine the outcome of the attempt. If the attempt is more than can be accomplished as a free action, they may also set an action cost for the attempt.

Examples: Use Stealth to hide; Use Awe to intimidate foes; Use Craft to improvise a barricade.

SPECIAL MOVEMENT

Climbing, crawling, swimming, navigating difficult terrain and any other inhibited movement all costs twice as much movement to accomplish. For example, swimming through 10 feet of water requires 20 feet of movement.

In general, you're able to move through space occupied by allies, but not through space occupied by foes or other obstacles. The GM has discretion to determine where you can and cannot move.

Flying combatants are able to move through the air up to their Speed, but if they are knocked prone, their speed is reduced to 0, or they are otherwise made unable to move, they fall to the ground.

PRONE

While prone:

  • You automatically lose engagements (see Engagement below).

  • Melee attacks against you are favored.

  • Your melee attack rolls are ill-favored.

  • Ranged attacks against you from further away than short range are ill-favored.

To stand up from prone, you must spend movement equal to half your Speed on your turn. Otherwise, your only movement option is to crawl. You may fall prone on your turn as a free action.

FALLING

Falling to the ground from a height deals 1d6 damage for every 10 feet fallen. Additionally, for every 20 feet fallen, roll Injury (see Injury below). For example, a creature that falls from a height of 40 feet would take 4d6 damage and roll Injury twice.

By default, a creature lands prone at the end of a fall. The GM may allow for a skill check (typically Dexterity) to attempt to land on your feet.

JUMPING, LIFTING, PUSHING, PULLING

You can jump a distance equal to your height from a standing position, or twice that distance with a running start of at least 10 feet. Either way, the maximum height of your jump is half your height, and the jump distance counts as movement.

You can lift, push or pull objects weighing up to your own weight.

The GM may allow you to attempt to exceed these limits with a skill check.

REACH & OPPORTUNITY ATTACKS

REACH is the distance at which a combatant can make melee attacks without moving from their current position. By default, combatants control a 5 foot square in combat and their reach extends to each of the 5 foot squares adjacent to their own. Larger or smaller combatants may take up more or less space and have longer or shorter reach.

Abilities and equipment that provide their own reach extend a combatant's existing reach. For example, a combatant with standard reach who is wielding a polearm with reach: 5 is able to attack foes who are TWO 5 ft squares out from their own.

Whenever one combatant leaves another's reach, the latter may use a reaction to make an opportunity attack: they make a single melee attack against them, immediately, skipping engagement (see Attacks & Damage and Engagement below).

DRAG, SHOVE & GRAPPLE

Attempting to drag, shove or grapple with a combatant is resolved via a contest - most often, Strength vs Strength.

Attacks against a grappled creature are favored. To attempt to escape a grapple, the creature may spend an action to repeat the original contest. On a win, they escape the grapple. On a loss, they remain grappled. See Special Statuses below.

COVER

If an obstacle completely blocks line of sight between an attacker and target for a melee or ranged attack, the attack cannot proceed. If half or more of the target is obscured, the attack is ill-favored. If less than half of the target is obscured, the attack proceeds as normal.

The GM may require a skill check to gain the benefits of cover in questionable circumstances.

SWITCHING WEAPONS

You may put away or pull out a weapon as a free action, as mentioned above. To put away one weapon and pull out another weapon, the cost is a half action. Alternately, you may drop a weapon as a free action, then pull out another weapon as a free action. As always, the GM may rule what can be reasonably accomplished with free actions during a turn.

DELAYING

You may delay your entire turn or a part of it. To do so, you must declare a specific trigger that will prompt your delayed turn (or part of it) and state exactly what you intend to do (e.g., “I will run to the south door if the ogre moves away from it.”). You may delay movement, part of your movement, or one or more actions, half actions, or free Actions.

When the declared trigger occurs, you immediately resolve the delayed turn or part of your turn. If the trigger does not occur before the end of the round, resolve the delay as follows:

  • If you delayed your entire turn, you take it at the end of the round.

  • If you delayed only part of your turn, that part is forfeited.

After resolving your delayed turn (or part of it), you rejoin your group in the initiative order in the next round of combat.

ATTACKS & DAMAGE

Any ability that inflicts harm or imposes the will of another on one or more unwilling creatures is considered an ATTACK. Attacks can employ many different mechanics, but most follow two common patterns:

  • The attacker rolls a skill check against a difficulty equal to one of the target’s stats (Defense is the default for melee and ranged attacks).

  • The attacker and target roll a contest against each other.

The skill check or the attacker's side of the contest are referred to as the attack roll for the attack.

Attacks have a wide range of effects when successful, but many attacks call for a damage roll:

DAMAGE ROLLS

The number and type(s) of dice rolled for a DAMAGE ROLL, as well as any modifiers applied, are determined by the ability and/or equipment used. The result of a damage roll is always subtracted from the target’s current Endurance.

Renaissance does not use explicit damage types. However, if the nature of the damage is relevant to the situation (e.g. A fire spell aimed at an ice golem), the GM may apply bonuses or penalties at their discretion—typically by adding or removing dice from the damage pool, or by doubling or halving the total damage (see Dice Rolls).

MARTIAL TRAINING

Anyone can pick up a sword, but knowing how to use it to good effect requires knowledge and experience. That knowledge and experience is represented by a character's MARTIAL TRAINING.

Each character is either trained or untrained in each category of equipment (see the Equipment section). Martial training is chiefly gained from a character's mestiere (see the Character Advancement section), but some abilities may impart additional martial training.

Whenever you make an attack with a weapon, if you are trained in its use, you may use it uninhibited: the attack roll is flat by default. If you are not trained in its use, the attack roll is ill-favored by default.

ATTACK TYPES

Each attack has a TYPE, which is informed by the equipment or ability used to make the attack, as well as the distance between the attacker and target(s). The attack type itself does not have any intrinsic effect, but various abilities in the game interact with, or are triggered by, specific attack types.

All physical attacks are classified as either melee attacks - those made via direct, physical contact - or ranged attacks - those made with a thrown or ranged weapon. A melee attack that benefits from augmented reach is still considered a melee attack. Any attack made with a weapon is also considered a weapon attack.

An attack made with a spell ability is considered a spell attack. An attack made with a magical weapon is a melee or ranged weapon attack, not a spell attack.

When these types intersect, they combine: an arrow shot from a bow is a ranged weapon attack, for example.

DEFAULT ATTACK MECHANICS

While various abilities and equipment may dictate different attack mechanics, melee and ranged attacks follow these default mechanics:

  • Melee attacks are made by rolling Strength against the target’s Defense.

  • Ranged attacks are made by rolling Dexterity against the target’s Defense.

  • Unarmed attacks or attacks using an improvised weapon use a single d4 for damage rolls on a hit, unless otherwise dictated by an ability or determined by the GM.

In all of the above cases, add your BODY score to the damage roll.

RANGE & RANGED ATTACKS

Many weapons, abilities and effects have a range, which is expressed in five tiers:

ADJACENT = up to 5 feet, or within reach, whichever is greater
SHORT RANGE = up to 25 feet
MEDIUM RANGE = up to 50 feet
LONG RANGE = up to 100 feet
FAR RANGE = up to 200 feet

Some abilities may indicate an effect of "+Range" or "-Range." This means upgrade or downgrade an existing range by one tier. Range cannot be reduced below Adjacent and cannot be increased beyond Far in this way, though other language like "double" or "halve" does not have the same limitation.

Ranged attacks against adjacent creatures are ill-favored if the creature can see you.

When attacking with a ranged weapon at short range or further, you may sacrifice accuracy for increased range. If the attack roll is not already ill-favored, you may make it ill-favored to double the weapon's range for the attack.

ENGAGEMENT

Melee combat is rarely a simple case of taking a swing with a weapon. More often, there is an exchange of careful maneuvers and footwork before an attacker attempts to land a blow. This exchange is represented by ENGAGEMENT.

Any time a combatant makes a melee attack, they and the target of the attack enter engagement, rolling engagement dice to determine the outcome of the exchange.

Each combatant has a limited number of engagement dice available to them each round. These dice are generally granted by their martial training and by equipment they're wearing or wielding. As such, combatants specializing in melee combat are likely to have far more engagement dice than those who specialize in other areas.

ENTERING ENGAGEMENT

Each combatant chooses which of their engagement dice they will roll for each engagement. Because engagement dice are a per-round resource, it may be advantageous to reserve some dice in anticipation of other engagements that may occur during within the round.

Once both sides have chosen their dice, count down from three and then roll all engagement dice simultaneously.

The number and types of the dice you’re committing to the engagement do not have to be declared before rolling. In fact, any and all methods of concealing your dice - or even deceptive tactics like shaking dice in your hand but not actually rolling them - are fair game.

RESOLVING ENGAGEMENT

Compare the highest die result from each side. The side with the higher result in that pair wins the pair. Then compare the next-highest pair, then the next-highest, and so on until all dice have been considered. The side with the most wins wins the engagement. If there is an equal number of wins on both sides, the engagement results in a draw.

If one combatant rolls more dice than the other, the unopposed dice count as wins. If one side decides not to roll any engagement dice, they automatically lose the engagement. If neither side rolled any dice, it's a draw.

As you resolve each pair of engagement dice, use the outcomes to describe the action and - at the end - how it positions the attacker to strike a blow.

Once the engagement is resolved, the attacker makes their Attack Roll:

  • If the attacker won the engagement, the attack roll is favored.

  • If the defender won the engagement, the attack roll is ill-Favored.

  • If the engagement resulted in a draw, the attack roll is unmodified. If it was a flat roll to begin with, it remains flat. If it was already favored or ill-favored, it remains so.

Describe how the attacker is positioned for their strike at the end of the engagement.

SPENDING & REGAINING ENGAGEMENT DICE

As soon as a die is rolled for engagement, it is considered spent and cannot be used again until it is regained. At the beginning of each combatant's turn, all their spent engagement dice are regained.

ENGAGEMENT EXAMPLE

An attacker spends an action to make a melee attack against an adjacent combatant. They enter engagement.

The attacker has a pool of five engagement dice available - four d6s from their mestiere and one d10 from the greatsword they're wielding. They want to have a good chance of winning the engagement, but they also expect a counter-attack before their next turn, so they choose to use the d8 and two of their d6s for this engagement, reserving the other two d6s.

The defender has a pool of just two engagement dice available - a d4 from their dagger and a d8 from their longsword. Their Endurance is very low at the moment and their turn is next - meaning their engagement dice will be regained - so they choose to use all of their available dice.

Both sides roll their dice simultaneously. As shown below, the attacker has rolled a 9 on a d10, a 5 on a d6 and a 1 on a second d6. The defender has rolled a 7 on a d8 and a 3 on a d4:

The 9 and 7 are the highest for each combatant, so we compare them and the attacker wins that pair. The 5 and 3 are the next-highest, so we compare them and, once again, the attacker wins. The remaining d6 from the attacker is unopposed, so that's another win. That's a 3-0 engagement victory for the attacker.

Now they can proceed with the attack roll, which is favored because they won the engagement. Both combatants cannot use the dice they rolled in another engagement until the dice are refreshed at the beginning of their next respective turns.

ENGAGEMENT SUCCESSES

Any time you roll the maximum result on an engagement die, you have won an ENGAGEMENT SUCCESS, which you can spend to achieve various effects during the current engagement. These are similar to but separate from the successes you can achieve with skill checks.

The effects available for you to purchase with engagement successes are determined by your martial training, your abilities, and by the equipment you're currently wielding or wearing. Each mestiere, ability or equipment item indicates which engagement success effects it makes available to you. Below are all available engagement success effects:

  • BIND - You and your opponent's weapons lock together. The engagement ends in a draw, immediately (the attack still proceeds).

  • COMPASS - You may move around your opponent to any position adjacent to them that you can reach through up to 10 ft of normal movement. This movement does not count against your normal per-round movement and does not provoke opportunity attacks.

  • DISARM - Your opponent drops a wielded item of your choosing. You may only use this if you have already used another success in this engagement.

  • FEINT  - You may re-roll one of your unresolved engagement dice.

  • HOOK - Choose one piece of your opponent's armor or their shield. They lose the benefits of that item until the start of their next turn. If they have no armor or a shield, they instead take -1 Defense until the start of their next turn.

  • INVITATION - Your opponent must re-roll an unresolved engagement die of your choice.

  • KNOCKBACK - You push your opponent 5 feet back. If this puts either of you outside the other's reach, the attacker in this engagement may use additional movement to move within reach. Otherwise, the engagement ends immediately and no attack is made. If this is the second time you've used Knockback in this engagement, the opponent is also knocked prone.

  • MANCHETTE - You land a glancing blow. Your opponent takes 1 Injury.

  • PARRY - You deflect your opponent's incoming maneuver. You win this pair, regardless of who has the higher die result. If your opponent also uses Parry for this pair, the higher die result wins as normal.

  • RETREAT - You move 5 feet away from your opponent. If this puts either of you outside the other's reach, the attacker in this engagement may use additional movement to move within reach. Otherwise, the engagement ends immediately and no attack is made.

  • RIPOSTE - Make a melee attack against your opponent immediately, skipping engagement, then return to this engagement. You may only use this if you have already used another engagement success in this engagement.

  • STUN - All of your opponent's unspent engagement dice become spent.

  • SUNDER - Choose one piece of your opponent's armor or their shield. That item's Defense bonus, if any, is permanently reduced by 1. If they have no armor or shield, or only natural armor, their current Defense is reduced by 1.

Resolve engagement successes as you evaluate the pairs they are in. When you evaluate a pair that includes an engagement success, the player who rolled the success declares the effect they will use and resolves that effect before resolving the pair. If both players rolled a success in a pair, resolve the higher success result first (there is a tie, flip a coin or roll other dice to break the tie).

If a die that produced an engagement success initially is forced to be re-rolled before it is resolved, the original engagement success is lost.

You don't have to match specific engagement dice with their specific engagement success effects. The available effects are pooled together and can be bought with successes from any of your engagement dice. For example, let's say you're wielding a shield that grants you a d4 engagement die and the Parry effect, as well as a war hammer that grants you a d6 engagement die and the Knockback effect. If you were to roll a 4 on the d4 or a 6 on the d6, you could spend that success on either Parry OR Knockback.

INJURY

While Endurance is easily lost and easily gained, INJURY represents more severe harm that is more difficult to inflict and more difficult to heal. Injury makes you more vulnerable to the Helpless state, which in turn makes it harder to regain Endurance by resting (see the Rest & Recovery section).

INFLICTING INJURY

While some abilities provide special ways to directly inflict Injury on a target, it is possible to inflict Injury with any melee or ranged weapon or unarmed attack. If the result of the attack roll includes Sol 🌞, the attacker inflicts Injury on the target, even if the overall result of the roll is a failure or loss.

Whenever Injury is inflicted, the target rolls a fate die:

  • On a 1-10, the result is added to the target’s current Injury score.

  • On Sol 🌞, the wound is insignificant - no Injury is inflicted.

  • On Morte 💀, the wound is dire - the target’s Injury score increases to equal their base Defense.

For player characters, Injury rolls that produce Sol 🌞 or Morte 💀 contribute to BANE/BOON for the Quest, and Morte 💀 triggers a Soft Move from GM (see the Quest Mechanics section).

RESISTING INJURY

If an attack inflicts Injury on a combatant and the they are not Helpless, before rolling for Injury, a they may choose to resist the Injury by checking a Condition: they heighten their emotions to avoid the worst of a blow. If they do so, they may roll two fate dice instead of one for their Injury roll and keep the more favorable result. They may only do this only once per Injury roll.

DEATH

KNOCKOUTS & DYING

When your Endurance is reduced to 0, you are knocked unconscious. You fall prone and drop any items you’re carrying that aren’t attached to your body. While unconscious, your Defense is reduced by your WITS score, to a minimum of 0. Armor and any other effects augmenting your Defense remain in place. Any time an unconscious creature is dealt damage, it also rolls Injury.

If you are not Twice Helpless, you wake up after an hour with 1 Endurance. If you are Twice Helpless and unconscious, you are dying: if you don’t return to at least 1 Endurance within an hour, you die.

Anyone may attempt to stabilize a creature that is dying by making an Aid check. The Difficulty is equal to the dying creature's current Injury score + 10. On a pass, they remain unconscious at 0 Endurance but are no longer dying.

An unconscious creature that regains at least 1 Endurance immediately wakes up. Any time you wake up from being knocked unconscious, check a Condition.

Damage never causes you to have negative Endurance - 0 is the minimum - but it is possible to die instantly. When damage reduces you to 0 Endurance and there is damage remaining, you die instantly if the remaining damage equals or exceeds your base Endurance.

If an attacker wants to knock a creature unconscious without risk of killing them, they must declare this intent before making their attack roll. If they reduce the creature to 0 Endurance, it falls unconscious, is stable, and will wake up in one hour with 1 Endurance.

SUFFOCATION & DROWNING

You can hold your breath for a number of seconds equal to twice your base Endurance, rounded up to the nearest 5 seconds. Once that limit is reached, you lose half your current Endurance, rounded up, each turn (or every 5 seconds if out of combat). If you reach 0 Endurance, follow the normal rules for knockouts and dying.

SPECIAL STATUSES

Various abilities, effects and combat actions impart SPECIAL STATUSES to combatants.

GRAPPLED

A creature that is grappled has a speed of 0. If they are grappled by another creature, they may spend an action to roll Strength vs Strength against the grappling creature. On a win, they are no longer grappled. On a loss, they remain grappled.

BLINDED

A creature that is blinded cannot see. It automatically loses engagement and fails/loses any skill checks that rely on sight.

PHASED OUT

Creatures and objects that are phased out are located in a separate plane of existence that is overlayed upon the physical world. While a creature or object is phased out:

  • It cannot be perceived by creatures or magical sensors located in the physical world.

  • It perceives the physical world in grayscale, and its vision becomes blurry beyond long range. Other phased out creatures and objects appear in full color and in focus as normal.

  • It cannot interact with the physical world, but can interact with other phased-out creatures and objects.

Entering or exiting the phased-out state immediately ends all concentration (see the Abilities section).

CHARMED

A charmed creature considers the person who charmed them to be a trustworthy friend and acts accordingly. Rolls made by the charmer to influence the charmed creature are favored.
